Built for speed, economy, and above all comfort, the Comet is powered by an Avanti AA-700 series propulsion system built around a quartet of variable-intake turbofans that offer excellent airspeed and maneuverability. Seating for the Comet's one hundred and twenty passengers is broken into two decks, with much of the upper deck devoted to two large first-class suites. These suites offer banquet facilities, private quarters convertible for personal and business meetings, and an office center providing access to the liner's onboard satellite and communications suite, enabling VIP passengers to enjoy the full range of local holovid, interweb, and telecommunications networks during their trip.

The ACL-800 comes equipped with inflatable lifeboats for emergency water landings and a small sick bay for minor medical crises in transit. The secure cargo stores located behind the lower passenger deck handle diverse cargos ranging from routine passenger luggage to small vehicles. Economy versions that dispense with the first-class suites can more than double the passenger and cargo capacity.

Avanti Aerospace of Canonbie, the primary branch of Avanti Industries, has been a longtime producer of civilian aircraft for the Lyran elite, with products ranging from the ACP series of private aircraft to the popular ACS Stratocruiser airship series. While most of these designs cater to the exceptionally wealthy, the ACL airliner series has set the standard for comfort and economy in commercial air travel across both halves of the former Federated Commonwealth, if not the whole of the Inner Sphere. Weighing in at one hundred and eighty tons, the ACL-800 Comet is the most common civilian airliner offered by Avanti Aerospace and the benchmark against which all competitors are measured.

All these features combined have earned the ACL class its place in airlines across the Steiner and Davion realms, and customized models have become popular as the private craft of planetary leaders and major corporate executives. The Comet's popularity has also led to a number of copies seen across the Inner Sphere, from licensed models to honest competitors to outright acts of corporate theft.

The ACL-800's dominance of the commercial air travel market drew both flattery and controversy. Michaelson Aircraft's MA-80 Delta Air Cruiser, seen in skies across the Federated Suns' Capellan March, is an Avanti-licensed model differing in only the most minor ways. Wakazashi's WK-1000 Stratos represents an honest effort by a corporate rival to match the ACL-800's specifications with a ninety-passenger design tailored to the Draconis Combine market.

Less welcome was the TC-80 Skyliner series recently debuted by St. Ives-based Mujika Aerospace. According to Avanti lawyers, the Skyliner sports engine designs almost indistinguishable from the Avanti AA-700, and legal action remains pending against Mujika for what Avanti characterizes as blatant corporate theft. Despite these imitators -- or perhaps because of them -- the ACL-800 Comet remains the standard against which all Inner Sphere commercial airliners are measured, a sign of the quality of Avanti's engineering and the enduring appeal of their design philosophy.

The Delta Air Cruiser retains the Comet's core strengths: a quartet of powerful variable-intake turbofans providing excellent airspeed and maneuverability, a two-deck passenger configuration with first-class amenities on the upper level, and the robust cargo storage behind the lower passenger deck. Michaelson's local adaptations are primarily cosmetic and logistical, ensuring that the aircraft can be serviced and maintained using components sourced from Capellan March suppliers rather than relying entirely on Canonbie-based Avanti parts chains. This localized supply network gives the Delta Air Cruiser a practical edge in its home market, reducing turnaround times for maintenance and keeping operating costs competitive.

The MA-80 carries the same one hundred and twenty passengers as the standard Comet, split across the same two-deck layout. First-class suites on the upper deck offer the full range of communications and entertainment amenities, while the lower deck provides comfortable economy seating and access to the secure cargo stores aft of the passenger cabin.

The MA-80 Delta Air Cruiser is a product of Michaelson Aircraft, produced under license from Avanti Aerospace for the commercial aviation market of the Federated Suns' Capellan March. As an Avanti-licensed model, the Delta Air Cruiser shares the fundamental design philosophy and proven engineering of the ACL-800 Comet, the most successful civilian airliner in the Inner Sphere, differing from its parent design in only the most minor ways. Michaelson secured the license during the Federated Commonwealth era, gaining access to a proven airframe while giving Avanti a manufacturing partner in a region far removed from their Canonbie production facilities. The arrangement has served both companies well, keeping the ACL platform dominant in the Capellan March's commercial aviation market.

The Delta Air Cruiser is a common sight in the skies across the Federated Suns' Capellan March, where it serves as the backbone of regional commercial air travel. Airlines operating in the March favor the MA-80 for its combination of Avanti's proven design with Michaelson's local support infrastructure. The aircraft serves routes connecting the March's major population centers and spaceports, providing reliable and comfortable transit for both civilian passengers and light commercial cargo.

Michaelson Aircraft secured its license from Avanti Aerospace during the Federated Commonwealth era, when the political and economic integration of the Lyran and Davion realms encouraged cross-border industrial partnerships. The licensing arrangement allowed Avanti to extend the ACL platform's market reach into regions where direct sales from Canonbie were impractical, while giving Michaelson access to a proven design without the enormous cost of developing a competing airliner from scratch.

The arrangement has endured through political upheavals, including the FedCom Civil War and the subsequent realignment of borders and trade relationships. Michaelson continues to produce the Delta Air Cruiser at a steady rate, and the aircraft remains one of the most visible symbols of continued Steiner-Davion industrial cooperation in the Capellan March. That the license has survived the dissolution of the Federated Commonwealth speaks to the strength of the commercial relationship underlying it -- both companies profit too handsomely to let politics interfere.

The KC-9 model, which debuted in 3053, is the pinnacle of its class, weighing in at the largest possible size for maximum cargo capacity. It sports a CBM-Festerling hydrogen fuel cell engine as its main power supply, replacing the Praht-450 internal combustion turbines used by the KC-5 and KC-6 models. A sophisticated onboard communications system, first introduced on the KC-6, is complemented by one high-capacity lift hoist and six tons of industrial-grade armor strong enough to withstand most heavy weapons. The aircraft features tilt-rotor wings for VSTOL landings in difficult terrains, allowing far swifter delivery than the shorter hops of the Karnov VTOL.

Though plans were floated to upgrade to Lockheed Skyshield armor, functionally similar to modern battlefield armor, the necessary structural modifications proved too costly to the craft's primary cargo mission, and the predicted KC-10 military model never saw production. Yet, even without dedicated military armor, the KC-9's six tons of industrial plating proved adequate for most threats encountered in rear-area logistics operations. The seventy-six-ton cargo capacity with full access to a military-grade lift hoist makes the King Karnov one of the most capable industrial air transports available in the Inner Sphere.

As a battlefield support vehicle, New Earth Trading Company's Karnov UR Transport is a craft whose origins lay shrouded in mystery. The New Earth-based company has long been known to completely lack VTOL manufacturing capabilities, yet no other firm has taken credit for the design. In 3001, Lyran-based Lockheed/CBM of Gibbs unveiled a heavy industrial air transport with design lines so similar to the lighter Karnov that corporate conspiracy theorists immediately declared the origin mystery solved. The mystery only deepened, however, as Lockheed/CBM insisted their KC-5 air transport was based on entirely different engineering. Though Lockheed/CBM maintained the KC series bore only a superficial resemblance to the Karnov VTOL, the aircraft was built for sustained long-distance air travel rather than the shorter hops of the VTOL, with engines and electronics wholly made in the Commonwealth.

Despite the lack of a dedicated military variant, sales of the KC-9 to military and militia units rose steadily throughout the Commonwealth states in the decade after the Clan Invasion, as the allies struggled to race troops and supplies to the front lines. The King Karnov competes with similar industrial air transports across the Inner Sphere, including Cal-Boeing's SA-10 Swallow favored in the Federated Suns and the AAC-60 Walrus produced by Andurien AeroTek for Free Worlds League, Capellan, and corporate agencies.

Despite Lockheed/CBM's protests, the media-dubbed King Karnov name stuck with the KC series, though it was never formally adopted by the company. A failed 3012 legal action by NETC charged that Lockheed/CBM had deliberately traded on the Karnov name. While Lockheed/CBM admitted their KC-5 bore a certain resemblance to the Karnov, they maintained it was built as an aircraft for sustained long-distance air travel rather than the shorter hops of the VTOL, with engines and electronics wholly made in the Commonwealth. The lawsuit was found without merit and dismissed.

The KC series underwent numerous upgrades over the years to compete with rival industrial transports. The KC-6 introduced a sophisticated communications system, while the KC-9 of 3053 represented a fundamental redesign with its CBM-Festerling hydrogen fuel cell engine and maximum-sized airframe. Throughout these evolutions, the King Karnov always retained its distinctive look and its association, however disputed, with the smaller Karnov VTOL. The aircraft's silhouette continues to invite comparison, and the King Karnov nickname has proven as enduring as the aircraft itself. The Lyran Alliance Armed Forces and later the LCAF made extensive use of the KC series for rear-area logistics, and the King Karnov eventually spawned enough specialized military variants that Lockheed/CBM developed the Zugvogel Omni Support Aircraft as a modular replacement capable of filling multiple roles from a single airframe.

 Lockheed/CBM Corp. Donegal Based on fluff TR:VAr 200.0

Intended for both military and civilian markets, the Longhaul has a strong hull capable of withstanding small-arms fire and even surviving heavier hits. It incorporates heavy-duty landing gear for rough-field operations, and four powerful fusion-turbine engines with thrust reversers for short field takeoffs and landings. Due to the high ground pressure of its compact landing gear, the Longhaul cannot use a completely unprepared field, though it does not take much for an engineering unit to clear and prepare a landing strip. These impressive qualities may not be required by civilian customers, but they ensure an aircraft capable of heavy use with few maintenance problems.

It is the Longhaul's cargo capacity that makes it such a valuable asset. Its mammoth cargo bay, with drive-on/drive-off loading ramps at front and back along with side personnel entry doors, has a capacity of one hundred tons. During prototype trials, it carried two Vedette tanks with support personnel, three Pegasus hovertanks that literally drove out of the rear as it rolled down the runway, and even an Atlas -- though the latter required significant effort to remove before it could walk off.

In the modern age, when the average person thinks of cargo transport, they likely picture a Mule or similar cargo DropShip. The DropShip is but one link in the extensive transport chain, however -- the only way to move cargo from one world to another. On-world, deepwater cargo ships, barges, trains, and trucks all play their parts, carrying heavy loads across long distances at a relatively slow rate. When cargoes must be delivered rapidly without resorting to the rare DropShip, conventional aircraft are the choice. The Federated-Boeing Longhaul represents the high end of mid-sized conventional cargo aircraft, the product of literally centuries of aerospace engineering experience from one of the largest corporations in the Inner Sphere.

On the strength of documented test footage showing all three of those remarkable prototype flights, local cargo companies on dozens of Federated Suns worlds purchased their own Longhauls. Military units frequently call on the craft to transport personnel or serve as a mobile command post. Dedicated Longhaul units typically maintain different modules that can rapidly convert the cavernous cargo hold into a multi-level configuration, carrying some seven hundred passengers while still having room for more than fifty tons of palletized gear.

The Longhaul has seen quite a few variations over the years. Most cargo hauler companies use it solely for freight, though military Longhauls are often called on to transport personnel or serve as mobile command posts. Federated-Boeing's painstaking documentation of every prototype test established the aircraft's reputation for reliability and capacity that competitors have struggled to match.

The Longhaul is a rugged design, but it is not indestructible, as accidents over the years have proven -- though most have been due to pilot error or misuse. Cargo must be secured properly or dangerous shifts can rip open the fuselage or destroy flight controls. The aircraft cannot constantly operate from short, temporary airfields with maximum cargo loads without regular heavy maintenance, or the landing gear will eventually collapse and the engines may fail on takeoff or landing. Steep landings are also problematic, and while the Longhaul can take to the air on a short runway, it still requires a fair amount of distance before reaching enough airspeed for a steep climb. These limitations are well understood by experienced crews, and the Longhaul's impressive overall service record speaks to the professionalism of those who fly and maintain it.

The S 2772 features a double-decked design that provides extraordinary interior volume for its class. Those on the lookout for a flying estate will find a whole customer market at their feet -- Branthhide sofas can be ordered from stock, five-star kitchens cater to every taste, small recreational parks, hot-spring bathing caverns, and carousels for children can all be incorporated, all at nearly supersonic speeds with or without an automatic landing system. Only the buyer's budget is the limit.

The aircraft cruises at high subsonic speeds, offering a smooth and quiet ride that allows passengers to enjoy these amenities in comfort during extended continental transit. The double-deck configuration separates service areas from living spaces, giving the aircraft the feel of a proper residence rather than a vehicle. SphereBAC's craftsmen handle every commission individually, and each S 2772 is effectively a unique creation, with no two interiors alike. The sheer mass of the aircraft -- among the heaviest civilian planes in regular production -- is both its greatest strength and its most significant limitation, as suitable runways are not always available at a buyer's preferred destination.

Once quite a fad among nobility, tycoons, and the nouveau riche, real luxury planes like the double-decked S 2772 outfitted by New Avalon-based SphereBAC have become few and far between. Expensive and difficult to maintain, and quickly outmoded both in fashion and technology, only the wealthiest with nothing else to care about treat themselves to such a pleasure. SphereBAC nonetheless carved out a niche serving the most exclusive clientele in the Inner Sphere, with their New Avalon workshops producing some of the most opulent aircraft ever to take flight. The S 2772 represents the pinnacle of atmospheric luxury -- a double-decked flying estate that caters to those for whom cost is no object and ostentation is a way of life.

The wealthiest category of buyers includes most of the Great Houses, especially the Davion Royal Household fleet of more than one hundred planes, with two aircraft kept ready for use on every major world in the Federated Suns. However, even this source of income for manufacturers tapered down as heads of state became more interested in security than opulence. Most successful businesses -- the other major customer segment -- tend to settle near spaceport hubs, making planetary travel a matter of short distances better served by VTOLs.

The decline of luxury planes like the S 2772 stems from both practical and financial causes. VTOLs carry a smaller price tag and offer much more flexibility, as not every customer, corporate headquarters, or resort has a runway readily available. The rise of recovered technology during the last decades of the thirty-first century only accelerated the trend. VTOLs became faster and, with recovered fusion technology, gained almost unlimited range. Rediscovered communication technologies allowed for better availability anywhere, eliminating the need for fast transit.

Perhaps the most damaging blow to the personal luxury plane market came from an unexpected quarter: the sudden prestige of private DropShips. With recovered Star League-era technology making private spacecraft more attainable for the ultra-wealthy, the allure of a mere atmospheric aircraft dimmed considerably. After all, who would still want a luxury jet when they now had a real chance at a private DropShip? Despite these pressures, SphereBAC has continued to serve its dwindling but fiercely loyal clientele from New Avalon, maintaining the S 2772 as the gold standard of atmospheric luxury for those who still appreciate the experience of flight itself.

The Stratos carries ninety passengers compared to the Comet's one hundred and twenty, a concession to the realities of designing without access to Avanti's proprietary AA-700 propulsion system. Wakazashi compensated by optimizing the aircraft's interior layout for efficiency, ensuring that the smaller passenger count does not translate to a proportionally smaller revenue stream. The Stratos offers a comfortable cabin with amenities competitive with the Comet's economy configuration, though it lacks the expansive first-class suites that define the ACL-800's upper deck. Wakazashi's own turbofan engines provide reliable performance, if not quite the refinement of the Avanti powerplants.

Where the Stratos gains ground against the Comet is in operational simplicity and maintenance. Wakazashi designed the aircraft with the Combine's existing aerospace maintenance infrastructure in mind, using standardized components that any licensed Wakazashi service center can repair or replace. This reduces downtime between flights and keeps operating costs predictable for the airlines that depend on the aircraft for daily revenue service.

The WK-1000 Stratos is Wakazashi Enterprises' entry into the commercial airliner market, designed to compete with Avanti Aerospace's dominant ACL-800 Comet. Unlike other Comet imitators that relied on licensing agreements or outright theft of Avanti's designs, Wakazashi developed the Stratos as an independent effort to match the ACL-800's specifications using Combine-sourced components and engineering. The result is a ninety-passenger airliner that, while smaller than the Comet, represents an honest attempt to challenge Avanti's near-monopoly on quality commercial air travel within the borders of the Draconis Combine. Wakazashi's corporate reputation as one of the Combine's premier aerospace manufacturers lent the Stratos immediate credibility in a market skeptical of foreign designs.

The Stratos finds its primary market within the Draconis Combine, where Wakazashi's extensive corporate network ensures ready access to parts and maintenance support. Airlines and planetary transit authorities across the Combine operate the WK-1000 on domestic routes, valuing its Combine-built pedigree and the independence from Avanti supply chains that it represents. Some Stratos airliners have found buyers in the Free Worlds League and Periphery states seeking a quality airliner without the political complications of purchasing from Steiner or Davion manufacturers.

Wakazashi Enterprises' decision to develop the Stratos independently, rather than pursuing a license from Avanti, reflected both corporate pride and strategic calculation. The Draconis Combine's industrial policy has long favored domestic production over foreign imports, and an Avanti-licensed airliner would have been a difficult sell to Kuritan airlines accustomed to buying Combine-made equipment. Wakazashi's reputation as one of the Combine's premier aerospace manufacturers gave the Stratos instant credibility in a market skeptical of foreign designs.

The Stratos debuted to respectable reviews, with aviation analysts praising Wakazashi's engineering while noting that the ninety-passenger capacity placed it at a disadvantage against the larger Comet on high-traffic routes. Yet, the WK-1000 carved out a solid niche in the Combine market and demonstrated that Wakazashi could produce more than military hardware and luxury aircraft like the Graceful Crane. Powered by an Edasich commercial-grade fusion engine, the Zugvogel is approximately twenty-five percent faster than the King Karnov it was designed to replace, with a cruising speed sufficient to keep pace with most ground offensives. Eleven and a half tons of military-grade armor rated at BAR 10 provides respectable protection for a support aircraft, while CASE reinforcement protects the crew and airframe against catastrophic ammunition detonation in armed configurations. An advanced fire control system enhances weapons accuracy across all configurations that carry offensive armament.

The aircraft's defining characteristic is its seventy-one and a half tons of available pod space. Five factory-produced OmniPod kits cover the most common mission profiles. The Prime configuration serves as a heavily armed combat transport, pairing forward-mounted missile launchers and light autocannons with a rear-facing light Gauss rifle and over twenty-three tons of cargo space. The A configuration transforms the aircraft into a flying command post packed with sensor suites and a C3 master computer capable of coordinating an entire planetary campaign. The B and C configurations fill medical and repair roles respectively, mounting a ten-theater MASH unit and mobile field repair bases. The D configuration, nicknamed the Raubvogel, serves as an aerial gunship mounting twin Gauss rifles and a heavy PPC capable of threatening heavy aerospace fighters.

The Zugvogel is a two-hundred-ton Omni support aircraft developed by Lockheed/CBM on Gibbs for the Lyran Commonwealth. Conceived during the post-Jihad reconstruction era to replace a bewildering array of modified King Karnov transports, the Zugvogel leverages OmniPod technology to fill nearly any support role from a single airframe. Where the LCAF Quartermaster Corps once required extensive factory retooling to produce specialized King Karnov variants, the Zugvogel can be reconfigured in the field through modular pod swaps. Its enormous pod capacity of over seventy tons allows it to mount weapons, sensors, medical facilities, or cargo space in virtually any combination, following the same consolidation philosophy that led to the Morgenstern OmniFighter.

The A configuration converts the Zugvogel into a fully equipped aerial command post. Multiple sensor suites including high-resolution, hyperspectral, and infrared imagers work alongside look-down radar to provide comprehensive battlefield awareness. A command console linked to a C3 master computer and extensive communications array enables a commanding officer to direct operations from the air, while rear-facing LB 2-X autocannons and a forward medium variable speed pulse laser provide minimal self-protection.

The LCAF and later the LAAF have long maintained one of the largest fixed-wing support aircraft fleets in the Inner Sphere. Lockheed/CBM's KC-9 King Karnov became a mainstay of Lyran logistic units following its debut in 3001, with the Quartermaster Corps requesting numerous modifications to the transport's spacious cargo bay over the decades. Gunship, bomber, mobile command post, and MASH conversions all saw limited production runs, but each required expensive factory retooling and dedicated manufacturing lines.

By the late Jihad era, Lockheed/CBM sought to address this inefficiency. Drawing inspiration from the success of their Morgenstern OmniFighter, which had replaced three separate aerospace fighter designs with a single modular airframe, the company applied OmniPod construction to the support aircraft role. The Zugvogel entered production on Gibbs in the early 3080s, with the plant having escaped the damage that crippled Lockheed/CBM facilities on Donegal and Tharkad during the Jihad.

The aircraft was still completing final quartermaster trials when it began attracting attention from multiple armed forces. The Third Skye CMR, a paratrooper-trained combat unit, was among the first to put the Zugvogel through operational testing during a series of RAF-LCAF war games. Using the mobile command post configuration to coordinate command and control while relying on the primary configuration for rapid paratrooper deployment, the regiment reportedly forced an entire combined arms battalion to surrender through a combination of aerial fire support and hit-and-run infantry tactics.

The Lyran Quartermaster Corps planned to requisition at least two hundred Zugvogels over the following five years, and interest extended beyond Lyran borders. The Republic of the Sphere and several other nations made inquiries about possible purchases once field trials concluded, suggesting the design may see broader adoption across the Inner Sphere.

The Caravan's primary asset is its cavernous sixty-ton cargo bay, accessible through four doors, two forward and two aft, enabling efficient loading and unloading of palletized freight or heavy military materiel. Powered by a primitive internal combustion engine, the aircraft achieves adequate cruising speed for continental-range cargo runs, though its primitive powerplant consumes fuel at a especially inefficient rate. Despite carrying thirteen tons of fuel, the Caravan's effective operational range is constrained by this thirst, and the fuel tanks themselves are fragile, lacking meaningful protective shielding.

Seven tons of BAR 6-rated armor provide reasonable protection for both the airframe and its cargo, though this mass serves as much a structural necessity for supporting heavy loads as it does a defensive measure. The Caravan carries no armament whatsoever, and its crew of three enlisted personnel have no ejection capability. These limitations were considered acceptable trade-offs for a civilian cargo platform never intended for hostile environments. The design's greatest operational strength is its ease of maintenance, a quality that kept Caravans flying for decades on frontier worlds with minimal technical support infrastructure.

The Caravan Heavy Transport is a 200-ton fixed-wing cargo aircraft designed by the Morrison-O'Connor-Marquand Corporation and introduced in 2346. Conceived during an era when atmospheric transport and space transport remained fundamentally separate industries, the Caravan filled a critical niche for planetary cargo hauling where DropShips and shuttles were either unavailable or prohibitively expensive. At 200 tons, it ranked among the largest conventional aircraft of its time, and its combination of massive cargo capacity, simple maintenance requirements, and low operating costs made it a favorite of civilian freight operators and government logistics agencies alike. The Caravan became one of the most commercially successful conventional aircraft designs in Inner Sphere history, with production expanding across multiple worlds to meet sustained demand throughout the Age of War.

The standard Caravan configuration saw service on hundreds of worlds across the Inner Sphere throughout the twenty-fourth and early twenty-fifth centuries, primarily operating from established airfields with long runway facilities capable of handling its 200-ton mass. Operators ranged from planetary government logistics agencies to private freight carriers, with the overwhelming majority serving purely civilian roles. Military use was limited and incidental, typically involving the transport of palletized supplies or heavy war materiel during wartime requisitioning rather than any dedicated combat logistics function. The aircraft's ubiquity ensured that trained maintenance crews and spare parts remained widely available throughout its operational life.

The Caravan proved an immediate commercial success following its 2346 debut, with more than ninety percent of all units sold to civilian and government operators rather than military customers. Demand grew so rapidly that Morrison-O'Connor-Marquand Corporation built primary production facilities on six different worlds, supplemented by final assembly plants on dozens more. The company organized a fleet of DropShips and JumpShips specifically to transport partially constructed Caravans from its factories to these assembly sites, creating one of the most extensive manufacturing and distribution networks for any conventional aircraft of the era.

Throughout the Age of War, the Caravan and similar large atmospheric transports dominated planetary cargo operations on virtually every major world. The design's combination of heavy lift capacity, low operating cost, and simple maintenance requirements made it indispensable to economies still reliant on conventional air transport for intra-planetary logistics. No military conflict of the period significantly disrupted this dominance, as the Caravan served a fundamentally civilian role that persisted regardless of which factions controlled the worlds where it operated.

The Caravan's decline came not from competition or conflict but from technological progress. As advances in spacecraft design brought the cost of DropShip and shuttle operations down to more accessible levels, the flexibility of space-capable transports made dedicated atmospheric cargo aircraft increasingly redundant. By the final decades of the twenty-fifth century, drop-shuttles and small DropShips had absorbed most of the roles the Caravan once filled. The design faded into obscurity by approximately 2490, and no single conventional aircraft design since has replicated its once-ubiquitous presence in planetary skies across the Inner Sphere.

The Boomerang's most obvious feature is its long wingspan. The tapering wings make it fuel-efficient and an excellent glide platform. Two forewings perched on thin spars of foamed aluminum promote control and stability, making the craft almost impervious to stalls. Two vertical stabilizers sit to either side of the cockpit; when in use, the entire stabilizer pivots rather than just the trailing edge, making the Boomerang extremely maneuverable.

The engine, a standard electric turbofan mounted below the cockpit floor, is highly efficient and quiet. Using over three thousand kilograms of fuel stored in the wings, the Boomerang achieves a range of almost five thousand kilometers, or more if the pilot glides. An unusual heat-bleeding system channels waste heat through slits on the upper wing edge, with the variable-pitched propeller dispersing it further, making the plane difficult to trace via infrared. The propeller can be feathered for virtually silent glide mode, and maximum ceiling with engine running is almost eighteen thousand meters.

The Boomerang carries over five hundred kilograms of reconnaissance gear, usually a pair of cameras with infrared and low-light capabilities that can work independently, locking on separate targets and relaying information to trailing radar planes or DropShips. The craft's major weakness is its complete lack of armament and armor, and pilots typically fly at three hundred meters or higher to stay out of danger.

Named for its distinctive V-shape, the Boomerang is representative of the spy planes used by the armed forces of the five Successor States. Designed by Cal-Boeing of Dorwinion on Filtvelt, the Boomerang was introduced in 2888 as the Federated Suns' standard reconnaissance plane and the first aircraft designed expressly for aerial reconnaissance in the Succession States era. Until then, civilian planes and their pilots were pressed into military service with mixed results. The Boomerang serves as a mobile spotter for artillery units and as a forward observer for advancing BattleMek formations, filling a critical intelligence-gathering role that no ground asset can match.

The Boomerang has performed long and well in service to the Federated Suns. Built with lightweight, low-maintenance materials, the plane has an excellent repair history. Most active duty regiments and planetary militias have at least one Boomerang in operational condition. Heavy-action units such as the Davion Brigade of Guards typically deploy up to fifteen Boomerangs during operational engagements. The Boomerang and most of its House counterparts can be easily disassembled and stowed in the holds of even the smallest DropShip. The only common complaint from technicians is the delicacy of the camera sensors, as heavily ionized or irradiated atmospheres tend to corrode them faster and degrade performance.

The lightweight Boomerang lacks many of the computer-guided systems common to larger aircraft, requiring its pilots to possess a natural flair for flying. The craft's unusual proportions posed challenges for its designers, particularly in developing suitable landing gear. Cal-Boeing chose to stow the nose gear below the fuselage and the long, thin landing wheels beneath the wings. Thanks to its large wingspan, the Boomerang requires only forty-four meters of landing space on a dry, level surface and seventy-five meters to take off.

As many variants exist as there are House militaries, with key differences lying mainly in silhouette and optics quality. The Capellan Dragonfly uses a knockoff Eo electric engine prone to shorting out after sustained G-force application. The Kuritan Shuriken has a smaller wingspan, necessitating longer runways. The Chariot retains the Protector's proven airframe and high-speed performance, including its Mach 3 burst capability and STOL operations through vectored-thrust wing-mounted engines. Where the Chariot differs significantly is in its medical configuration. Rather than replicating the Protector's ten individual paramedic stations, Ceres Metals replaced the paramedic bays with a single-theater MASH module. In 3031, Ceres Metals Industries released the Chariot High-Speed Medevac, a Capellan-produced derivative of the Wangker AeroSpace C-790 Protector. A number of Protectors had been captured by Capellan forces during the Fourth Succession War, and Ceres wasted little time in reverse-engineering the aircraft for domestic production. The Chariot was intended to fill the Confederation's desperate need for high-speed medical evacuation aircraft, a capability that had been sorely lacking during the devastating Fourth War. Rather than produce a direct copy, however, Ceres made deliberate modifications that reflected the Confederation's own military medical doctrine and the harsh realities of its limited trained personnel.

The Chariot serves primarily with CCAF medical units and Capellan planetary garrisons, where it provides rapid casualty evacuation from forward engagement zones. Using a SISO (Slide In/Slide Out) module system similar to that found in the Cortez exploration vehicle, the Mosquito could be reconfigured to fit whatever research protocols were called for by the client. Airborne radar has been a mainstay in ground military units since the birth of atmospheric flight in the twentieth century. With the exploration and colonization boom in subsequent centuries, new uses for military-oriented technologies became evident. High-altitude spy planes became topographical tools for new worlds, and radar planes helped colonial scientists ascertain planetary details such as magnetic field strength, fault lines, tidal patterns, and local fauna migratory patterns. Essentially, old mothballed military equipment got a second wind as research platforms for the Age of Colonization. The Mosquito series of radar aircraft, first developed by DMI, Ltd. and later perfected by the Malrite Company, became one of the most successful and enduring examples of this trend, serving continuously from the mid-twenty-fifth century to the present day.

Mosquito planes can still be found in active service on most civilized systems. Common uses around the Inner Sphere see Mosquitos serving as firefighting planes, refueling platforms, storm chasers, and even as part of planetary defense forces. DMI, Ltd., found new life when the demand for their Walrus-class cargo haulers collapsed after Imstar Aerospace debuted their much cheaper and inherently safer Planetlifter Air Transport. Colonization corporations, planetary governments, and even several provincial militaries gobbled up every Mosquito that rolled off the assembly line. The unification of the Federation of Skye, Protectorate of Donegal, and Tamar Pact into the Lyran Commonwealth brought economic opportunity and political chaos in equal measure. Defense manufacturers throughout the new Commonwealth capitalized on the political uncertainty, and Edasich Aerospace Corporation was among the most aggressive. At just twenty tons, the ICE-powered Colt was built for speed and persistence rather than raw hitting power.

Colt sales were steady enough for Edasich Aerospace to maintain production as planetary militias and private security concerns across the Commonwealth prepared for the worst. The Colt's fortunes changed dramatically when Robert Marsden assumed the title of Archon Basileus and began a rapid expansion of the Lyran Commonwealth Armed Forces. Within just a few years, images of Colts attacking rebel positions on Skye and Tamar became iconic symbols of Marsden's consolidation of power.

This association with Lyran authority ensured the Colt's long service within the Commonwealth's air forces. Even as newer and more capable designs entered production, the Colt remained a fixture of planetary militias and garrison commands, valued for the same qualities of speed and endurance that had defined it from the beginning. Edasich Aerospace continued to support the design with spare parts and technical assistance for decades, cementing a profitable relationship with the LCAF that would sustain the company through multiple economic cycles.

The Mosquito Light Fighter is a primitive conventional fighter designed by AeroTech Industries of Andurien in 2302, at the dawn of the Age of War. Conceived as an affordable interceptor for the budget-conscious militaries of the era, the Mosquito filled an important niche as smaller powers throughout the Inner Sphere scrambled to equip their armed forces. The design earned a reputation for reliability and ease of maintenance, qualities that drove widespread adoption across multiple states and minor powers. Its commercial success established AeroTech Industries as one of the more prominent military aircraft producers of the twenty-third century, laying the groundwork for the company's evolution into an interstellar defense conglomerate.

The Mosquito saw its widest service among the armies and militias of the Capellan Confederation and Free Worlds League during the Age of War, where the contested border between the two states ensured constant demand for affordable combat aircraft. The late twenty-third century was a period of intense military buildup across the Inner Sphere, as the Great Houses consolidated power and smaller states fought for control of individual worlds. AeroTech Industries, headquartered on the beleaguered world of Andurien, had the dual benefit of witnessing firsthand the capabilities of its designs and a built-in customer base of defenders who desperately needed additional fighters. The company sold tens of thousands of Mosquitos throughout what would become the Capellan Confederation and Free Worlds League, additionally granting production licenses to nearly a dozen other concerns.
